title: How a Medical Loan Works and What It Costs
metaDescription: Interest rates on a medical loan vary sharply by credit tier, and a provider's own payment plan is usually cheaper.
cardBlurb: What a medical loan costs across credit tiers and how to avoid the retroactive interest trap on healthcare financing.
introText: A medical loan is borrowing used to pay healthcare expenses, typically taking the shape of a general personal loan, a provider-arranged installment plan, or a specialized healthcare credit card. At ModernWallet, we often see borrowers turn to third-party medical debt before checking whether their provider offers an interest-free billing arrangement directly. Commercial lenders offer rapid funding when you face unexpected care costs. Converting healthcare debt into standard consumer credit, however, strips away specific credit bureau protections and adds interest costs that a hospital billing office might never charge.

sections.heading: Financing Structures for Medical Bills
sections.body:
A medical loan usually refers to one of three financing structures used to cover healthcare costs. An unsecured personal loan provides a lump sum from an independent bank, credit union, or online lender. You receive the funds, pay the hospital directly, and repay the balance through fixed monthly installments over a set term.

A provider-arranged installment loan is offered at the clinic or hospital through a partnership with an outside financial company. The paperwork happens in the billing office, but a third-party lender manages the account and collects your payments.

A medical credit card is a revolving line of credit dedicated to healthcare expenses. Providers often market cards like [CareCredit](https://www.carecredit.com/) at the point of service to finance procedures not fully covered by insurance. The [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-should-i-know-about-medical-credit-cards-and-payment-plans-for-medical-bills-en-1827/) (CFPB) notes that each financing structure carries different interest terms and repayment obligations. Some options carry heavy risks. Confirm the loan structure in writing before you sign any paperwork in a provider's office.

sections.heading: Deferred Interest on Medical Credit Cards
sections.body:
Deferred interest on a medical credit card charges full retroactive interest from the original transaction date if you leave any balance unpaid when the promotional term expires. Promotional periods typically run from 6 to 24 months. Marketing materials often label these offers as zero percent interest, but deferred interest differs fundamentally from a true zero percent annual percentage rate (APR) promotion. If you carry even one dollar past the promotional deadline, the lender calculates interest retroactively on your entire original balance from the purchase date. The penalty is severe.

The CFPB's May 2023 [report on medical financing](https://files.consumerfinance.gov/f/documents/cfpb_medical-credit-cards-and-financing-plans_2023-05.pdf) revealed that deferred-interest healthcare financing terms frequently carried regular APRs as high as 26.99% once the promotional window expired. The report found that consumers used deferred-interest medical credit cards and installment plans for close to $23 billion in healthcare expenses across more than 17 million transactions between 2018 and 2020. Those borrowers paid roughly $1 billion in deferred interest during that three-year window.

Run the arithmetic on a $3,000 dental procedure with a 12-month deferred interest promotion at 26.99% APR. Suppose you make regular payments and reduce the principal to $200 by the end of month twelve. If month thirteen arrives with that $200 outstanding, your lender does not charge interest on the $200 balance alone. The lender charges 26.99% APR on the entire $3,000 starting from the original purchase date. That single misstep adds hundreds of dollars in retroactive finance charges to your account instantly. You can model monthly payments on our [credit card payoff calculator](/credit-card-payoff/) to ensure you clear the balance well ahead of promotional deadlines.

sections.heading: Medical Loan Costs by Credit Tier
sections.body:
The interest rate on an unsecured medical loan depends primarily on your credit score and the lender's underwriting standards. General-purpose personal loans carry fixed interest rates and predictable monthly schedules. Data from lender-rate surveys reported by [Experian](https://www.experian.com/blogs/ask-experian/best-personal-loan-rates/) shows that average personal loan APRs vary sharply by credit tier. At 760 or higher, you land in the 7% to 10% range. At 720 to 759, expect 10% to 14%. At 680 to 719, rates run 14% to 20%. At 640 to 679, they climb to 20% to 28%. Below 640, you face 26% to 36%. Rates climb fast for lower tiers. The [Federal Reserve](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/) publishes its G.19 Consumer Credit report as a broad national benchmark tracking average finance rates that commercial lenders charge on personal loans. Checking this benchmark gives you an objective baseline to compare against any rate a healthcare lender quotes.

If an unsecured rate is too steep, a secured loan offers an alternative. The [CFPB personal loans guide](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/consumer-tools/personal-loans/) points out that a secured loan requires collateral, such as a vehicle title or a savings account. Pledging collateral reduces the lender's risk and generally earns you a lower APR than an unsecured medical loan. The risk transfers to you, however, because the lender can seize your asset if you default. You can compare terms in our guide on [secured vs. unsecured loan](/compare/secured-vs-unsecured-loan/) tradeoffs or calculate monthly payments using our [personal loan calculator](/personal-loan/).

sections.heading: Credit Reporting Rules for Medical Debt
sections.body:
Converting an unpaid medical bill into a commercial loan eliminates the specialized credit reporting protections created for healthcare bills. Direct healthcare debt receives specific protections that do not apply to regular credit accounts. Starting in 2022 and 2023, the three nationwide credit bureaus, [Equifax](https://www.equifax.com/), Experian, and [TransUnion](https://www.transunion.com/), voluntarily updated their credit reporting rules. Paid medical collection debt is no longer included on consumer credit reports regardless of how long it took to satisfy the bill. Unpaid medical collection accounts under $500 are also excluded entirely. In addition, credit bureaus enforce a 365-day waiting period before any new medical debt can appear on a credit report, giving you time to resolve insurance disputes and billing errors.

Legal rules around medical reporting faced major challenges in court. The CFPB finalized a federal regulation in January 2025 under [Regulation V](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/final-rules/prohibition-on-creditors-and-consumer-reporting-agencies-concerning-medical-information-regulation-v/) that would have barred all medical debt from credit reports and credit evaluations. In July 2025, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas vacated that regulation in Cornerstone Credit Union League v. CFPB, determining that the rule exceeded statutory authority under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. As a result, the federal ban is not in effect. You rely strictly on the voluntary policies maintained by Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.

A commercial loan carries no grace period. When you pay a medical bill with a personal loan or credit card, the account is classified as standard consumer debt. If you fall behind on payments, the lender reports delinquent balances under standard credit reporting guidelines. You lose the under-$500 protection and the 365-day waiting period immediately. Missing a personal loan payment damages your credit profile far faster than negotiating an unresolved bill directly with a clinic.

sections.heading: Alternatives to Commercial Medical Lending
sections.body:
Hospital billing departments and nonprofit assistance funds provide lower-cost alternatives to commercial borrowing. Always ask the hospital first. Direct provider payment plans are frequently interest-free or low-interest, according to the CFPB. Because you arrange the agreement directly with the healthcare facility rather than a third-party financial firm, you avoid origination fees, compound interest, and aggressive collection tactics. Request an extended repayment schedule that fits your monthly cash flow before exploring external borrowing.

Many patients qualify for charity care without realizing it. Under Section 501(r) of the Internal Revenue Code, the [Internal Revenue Service](https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/financial-assistance-policy-and-emergency-medical-care-policy-section-501r4) (IRS) requires all nonprofit hospitals to maintain a written financial assistance policy. These programs reduce or forgive medical bills entirely for patients who earn below specific household income thresholds. Ask the billing department for its financial assistance application and fee schedule before paying a single dollar.

A credit card with a true introductory zero percent APR offers another route if you need extra time to pay. Unlike deferred-interest medical cards, standard zero percent promotional cards do not charge retroactive interest if a modest balance remains when the promotion ends. You only pay interest on the remaining unpaid portion going forward. Review our guide on [how to choose a balance transfer credit card](/guides/how-to-choose-a-balance-transfer-credit-card/) to understand how intro periods work and when transfer fees apply.

sections.heading: Borrowing Strategies for Fair or Poor Credit
sections.body:
Applying for medical financing with a fair or poor credit score requires strategies that protect your score from unnecessary damage. Prequalification saves your score. When shopping for an unsecured personal loan, look for lenders that offer prequalification using a soft credit inquiry. A soft pull allows you to review potential interest rates and loan terms without affecting your credit score. Only agree to a hard credit pull once you find an acceptable offer and prepare to submit the final application.

Adding a creditworthy co-signer can dramatically improve your loan terms. A co-signer with excellent credit reduces the lender's default risk, helping you secure an APR in the 7% to 14% range instead of the 20% to 36% rates common for lower credit tiers. Keep in mind that your co-signer assumes full legal liability for the balance if you miss a payment.

If an unsecured loan is unattainable or too expensive, a secured loan provides a viable alternative. Pledging a vehicle title or a savings certificate can help you qualify for lower rates even with damaged credit. Make sure the monthly payment is sustainable within your household budget by running your numbers through our [budget calculator](/budget/) and planning ahead with our [personal loan extra payment calculator](/personal-loan/extra-payment-calculator/).

sections.heading: Situations Where a Medical Loan Fails
sections.body:
A commercial medical loan is the wrong choice if your household income qualifies for hospital financial assistance or if the provider offers an in-house installment plan. Never borrow to pay an unverified bill. Taking out a loan to pay a medical bill before reviewing an itemized statement is a common mistake. Billing statements frequently contain coding errors, duplicate charges, or unapplied insurance discounts. If you pay the provider immediately with loan proceeds, you lose leverage to dispute inaccurate charges later.

A medical loan also fails anyone eligible for Section 501(r) hospital charity care. Exchanging an uncollected bill that could be forgiven or discounted for a commercial personal loan charging 14% to 28% APR creates unnecessary debt. Exhaust all financial assistance forms and dispute processes before considering any loan.

In addition, avoid third-party financing if the medical provider offers an internal payment arrangement with zero interest. Even a competitive 8% personal loan costs more than an in-house arrangement that charges no interest at all. Turn down outside financing whenever the clinic allows you to pay them directly over time.

sections.heading: Factors That Shift the Lending Decision
sections.body:
Our recommendation shifts toward a personal medical loan when a provider refuses an in-house payment plan and offers only a high-interest deferred financing card. If a clinic demands immediate payment and only offers a deferred-interest card with a 26.99% post-promotional APR, taking a fixed-rate personal loan from an independent lender is often the safer choice. A fixed-rate loan protects you from the retroactive interest trap, establishing a clear payoff date and a fixed monthly payment that never changes.

Your decision also changes if you have collateral that allows you to access a secured personal loan at a single-digit rate. When a hospital refuses to negotiate its total bill or offer low-cost monthly installments, financing the cost through a low-rate secured loan can be cheaper than letting the account slide toward collections.

Check the numbers before borrowing. Before signing for a medical loan, request an itemized billing statement and compare your prequalified personal loan offers against your provider's written payment terms. This guide provides general educational information rather than individualized financial or medical-billing advice, so verify all terms directly with your lender, insurer, or healthcare provider before agreeing to financing.

faqs.question: What is a medical loan?
faqs.answer: A medical loan is any debt product used to pay healthcare expenses, most commonly an unsecured personal loan, an installment loan through a provider partner, or a specialized healthcare credit card. Unsecured personal loans offer fixed rates and terms, while medical credit cards often feature deferred-interest promotional windows.

faqs.question: Is a medical credit card the same as a medical loan?
faqs.answer: No. A medical credit card is a revolving line of credit that frequently uses deferred interest promotions, whereas a standard medical loan is an installment loan with a fixed APR and set term. If you fail to pay off a medical credit card within the promotional window, interest is charged retroactively on the entire original balance.

faqs.question: How does a medical loan affect my credit score?
faqs.answer: A medical loan affects your credit score like any standard personal loan or credit card, without the protections granted to direct medical debt. It reports on-time payments, hard inquiries, and delinquencies directly to credit bureaus under standard commercial reporting guidelines.

faqs.question: Can I get a medical loan with bad credit?
faqs.answer: Yes, but you will face higher interest rates ranging from 20% to 36% APR. Borrowers with poor credit can improve their approval terms by using a creditworthy co-signer or applying for a secured loan backed by collateral such as a vehicle or savings account.

faqs.question: Is medical debt removed from credit reports?
faqs.answer: Paid medical collection debt and unpaid collections under $500 are excluded from credit reports under voluntary policies by Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. A separate federal regulation that would have banned all medical debt from credit reports was vacated by a federal court in July 2025 and is not in effect.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a medical loan and a hospital payment plan?
faqs.answer: A hospital payment plan is arranged directly with the provider's billing department and is frequently interest-free, while a medical loan is issued by a third-party commercial lender that charges interest and reports payment activity under standard credit guidelines.
